newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British academic explains BSE report.
newsitem.headline: British academic explains BSE report.

text.p: A report put to the British government and EU scientists suggests that mad cow disease could almost disappear by 2001 without culling more cattle, said Professor Roy Anderson of Oxford University.
Anderson, co-author of a controversial Oxford Report on the disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), was giving evidence on Tuesday to a European Parliament committee of inquiry.

Asked about the British government's commitment at the Florence EU summit to introduce an additional culling programme he replied, "In my own view that would do little to speed the elimination of the infectious agent."
The extra cull would cover up to 150,000 animals mkost at risk to BSE.
Anderson's report, which was announced in August, was only given to the British government and the EU's Scientific and Veterinary Committee three week's ago.
He said that the existing programme of killing all animals over 30 months old should be reorganised.
If cattle were slaughtered by age and specific herds and specific farms targeted then the number of BSE cases could be reduced to a trickle by early or mid-1998, he said.

"That is the fastest possible time period. You have to look at the practicalities and if a programme to slaughter all animals in infected herds were introduced there is not the capacity to deal with them any quicker," he told the inquiry.
Politicians who wanted to see a larger culling programme would have to be prepared to pay the cost, he said.
"The slaughter of an additional 150,000 animals would have a minimal effect and that is a scientific fact," he said.
He told MEPs that it was impossible to rule out the possibility that the fifteen cases of Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease (CJD), the human equivalent of BSE, might be the start of a massive epidemic.

"I strongly disagree with scientific statements on the future of the CJD epidemic. We have 15 cases and only a fool would attempt to forecast the future. We will not know what the pattern is likely to be for a number of years yet," he warned.

Anderson added that the EU must carry out further research into scrapie, a disease endemic in sheep, and its links with BSE. It must also examine the question of feeding animal protein to other animals.
